2026-03-13.teaser: Today's collection spans the full spectrum of technological disruption and its real-world consequences. We've got breakthrough energy plays that could reshape manufacturing, shocking security breaches that expose the vulnerability of enterprise AI systems, and deep dives into how entire industries operate in regulatory gray zones. From Chinese AI companies building on open-source foundations to the shadowy economics of online gaming, these stories reveal the messy, complex reality behind the headlines. Each piece offers something you won't find in your typical tech coverage.

included.title: How We Hacked McKinsey's AI Platform
included.source: X/Twitter bookmark via Dr Efi Pylarinou
included.summary: A security research team at CodeWall.AI successfully breached McKinsey's enterprise AI platform, Lilly, using autonomous agents to access massive amounts of sensitive data without authentication. The hack exposed 46.5 million chat messages and revealed fundamental security vulnerabilities in enterprise AI systems that are increasingly trusted with confidential business information. The breach highlights a critical gap between the rapid deployment of AI platforms and the implementation of robust security measures. The autonomous nature of the attack demonstrates how AI tools can be weaponized against AI systems, creating new categories of cyber threats. The scale of accessible data suggests that many organizations may be unknowingly exposing sensitive information through poorly secured AI interfaces. This incident raises urgent questions about data governance, authentication protocols, and the security architecture of enterprise AI platforms that handle confidential business communications and strategic information.

included.title: The Shadow Economy of Online Gaming: How Money Moves Beyond the Screen
included.summary: An investigative report reveals how banks, payment processors, and aggregators collaborated to enable transactions for shadow gaming operators by disguising them as legitimate e-commerce merchants. The investigation exposes a sophisticated network where gaming companies that couldn't secure direct payment processing relationships were quietly onboarded through alternative channels, circumventing regulatory oversight and compliance requirements. This shadow payment ecosystem allowed potentially illegal or unregulated gaming operations to process billions in transactions while appearing as standard retail businesses to financial institutions. The report details how payment aggregators served as intermediaries, creating layers of obfuscation that made it difficult for banks to identify the true nature of the underlying businesses. The investigation raises serious questions about due diligence practices in the payments industry and the effectiveness of current regulatory frameworks in monitoring high-risk sectors. The findings have implications for anti-money laundering compliance, consumer protection, and the broader integrity of digital payment systems that increasingly power the global economy.

included.title: OpenClaw: China's AI Stack
included.summary: Zhipu's launch of AutoClaw represents the culmination of a remarkable trend where every major Chinese AI company has built products around a single open-source project, creating an ecosystem that includes Moonshot's KimiClaw, MiniMax's MaxClaw, Alibaba's CoPaw, ByteDance's ArkClaw, and Tencent's WorkBuddy. This convergence around one foundational technology demonstrates how open-source projects can become the backbone of an entire national AI strategy, creating both opportunities and dependencies. The market response was immediate, with Zhipu's stock jumping 13% on the announcement, indicating investor confidence in this approach to AI development. This phenomenon highlights the power of open-source in democratizing AI capabilities while raising questions about technological sovereignty and the concentration of innovation around specific platforms. The Chinese AI companies' collective embrace of this technology stack suggests a coordinated approach to building competitive AI products without reinventing fundamental infrastructure. This strategy could accelerate innovation by allowing companies to focus on application-layer differentiation while sharing underlying technological foundations, though it also creates potential single points of failure for the entire ecosystem.

included.title: Swift Solar Acquires Meyer Burger to Build Gigawatt-Scale Solar Factory
included.summary: Swift Solar's acquisition of Meyer Burger represents a strategic shift from component supplier to end-product manufacturer, embodying the principle that superior technology should be used to compete directly rather than simply sold to others. Joel Jean at Swift Solar is applying this philosophy to solar manufacturing, using their advanced perovskite tandem solar cell technology to build a gigawatt-scale factory capable of producing highly efficient solar panels. The deal gives Swift Solar access to Meyer Burger's established manufacturing infrastructure and expertise, allowing them to scale their innovative technology rapidly. This vertical integration strategy challenges the traditional model where technology companies license their innovations to manufacturers, instead betting that controlling the entire value chain will create sustainable competitive advantages. The gigawatt-scale ambition signals Swift Solar's intention to compete directly with established solar panel manufacturers while leveraging their technological edge in efficiency. This approach could accelerate the adoption of next-generation solar technology by removing the intermediary step of technology licensing and ensuring that the most advanced innovations reach the market quickly. The acquisition demonstrates how breakthrough energy technologies are increasingly being paired with aggressive scaling strategies.

included.title: ITR Forms AY 2025-26: More Disclosures, Details on HRA, Home Loan, TDS
included.summary: India's new ITR forms for Assessment Year 2025-26 introduce significant changes that expand disclosure requirements and modify filing procedures for taxpayers. The most substantial change raises the asset disclosure threshold from ₹50 lakh to ₹1 crore in income, requiring high earners to provide comprehensive details of all assets in Schedule AL. This change affects a smaller but wealthier segment of taxpayers while reducing compliance burden for middle-income earners. The forms now allow taxpayers with long-term capital gains below ₹1.25 lakh to use simplified ITR-1 or ITR-4 forms, streamlining the filing process for small investors. Enhanced requirements for HRA and deduction details provide tax authorities with more granular information about common tax-saving claims, potentially improving compliance monitoring. A crucial addition requires separate reporting of capital gains before and after July 23, 2024, corresponding to budget changes that likely affected tax rates or exemptions. These modifications reflect the tax authority's dual approach of simplifying procedures for smaller taxpayers while increasing scrutiny and disclosure requirements for high-income individuals. The changes demonstrate India's evolving tax administration strategy, balancing ease of compliance with improved revenue collection and taxpayer monitoring.

included.title: Sarvam: Open is not sovereign
included.summary: This analysis challenges the conventional wisdom that open-source AI models automatically confer technological sovereignty, using Sarvam as a case study to examine the complex relationship between openness and independence in AI development. The piece argues that while open-source models provide access to code and weights, true sovereignty requires control over the entire AI value chain, including data, compute infrastructure, talent, and the ability to modify and improve foundational models independently. The author contends that countries and companies relying heavily on open-source models from foreign entities may actually be increasing their technological dependence rather than achieving independence. The analysis explores how Sarvam's approach to building AI capabilities intersects with broader questions about national AI strategies and the trade-offs between leveraging global open-source resources and developing indigenous capabilities. The piece examines whether open-source AI creates a false sense of technological autonomy while potentially deepening dependencies on the ecosystems, tools, and platforms controlled by the original model creators. This perspective challenges policymakers and technologists to think more critically about what genuine AI sovereignty requires in an increasingly interconnected global technology landscape.

2026-03-14.teaser: The financial world is buzzing with whispers of the next potential crisis, and it's not coming from where you might expect. Private credit markets are showing cracks that have seasoned fund managers issuing stark warnings about doubling default rates. When Swiss asset managers overseeing $180 billion start sounding alarms publicly, it's time to pay attention. This isn't just another market hiccup—it's a fundamental shift in how credit flows through the global economy. Today we dive deep into the mechanics of this shadow banking phenomenon and why its troubles could ripple far beyond Wall Street. Buckle up for a masterclass in modern finance's newest vulnerability.

included.title: What's going on with private credit? | Who said what? S2E34
included.summary: The private credit market is experiencing significant turbulence that has industry veterans comparing it to potential systemic risks. Steffen Meister from Partners Group, managing over $180 billion, warned that default rates could double in coming years—a stark assessment that signals deeper structural issues. The article expertly contextualizes private credit's emergence as an alternative to traditional banking, explaining how it fills gaps left by post-2008 regulatory constraints on banks. Unlike traditional lending where banks use short-term deposits for long-term loans, private credit funds match investor capital with borrower needs more directly. However, this shadow banking system now faces stress tests as economic conditions tighten. The piece illuminates how private credit became a $1.7 trillion market by offering higher yields to investors and more flexible terms to borrowers, particularly middle-market companies shut out of public bond markets. But with funds freezing withdrawals and assets being marked down, the sector's rapid growth may have outpaced its risk management capabilities. The analysis reveals how regulatory arbitrage created this parallel lending universe, but also suggests that what goes around comes around—the same market forces that enabled private credit's rise may now threaten its stability.

2026-03-15.teaser: Sometimes the most extraordinary business empires emerge not from grand visions, but from relentless focus on fundamentals. Today we explore how obsessive attention to controllable variables can transform a humble root beer stand into a global hospitality giant. The story reveals why fighting against expansion might be the secret to sustainable growth, and how mastering downside risk can turn economic downturns into competitive advantages. It's a masterclass in building without blueprints, where success comes not from predicting the future, but from creating systems robust enough to thrive in any future. The lessons here apply far beyond hospitality—they're about the patient art of empire-building through disciplined execution.

included.title: [Outliers] J.W. Marriott: Building an Empire Without a Master Plan
included.summary: This fascinating deep dive into Bill Marriott's business philosophy reveals how the world's largest hotel empire emerged from counterintuitive principles. Starting with a nine-seat root beer stand in Washington, DC, Marriott's journey to hospitality dominance wasn't driven by grand strategic vision but by obsessive focus on controllable variables and downside risk management. The most striking aspect? He actively resisted entering the hotel business until age 55, preferring to master adjacent markets first—including pioneering the airline catering industry. Marriott's approach centered on isolating variables like location selection and refusing to depend on forces beyond his control. This disciplined methodology allowed his company to expand during the Great Depression while competitors collapsed. The episode illuminates how sustainable empire-building often requires fighting your own growth instincts, choosing depth over breadth, and building systems robust enough to thrive regardless of external conditions. Rather than betting on market predictions, Marriott created a machine optimized for serving people well—a deceptively simple goal that became the foundation for extraordinary scale. His story challenges conventional wisdom about entrepreneurial ambition, suggesting that the most enduring businesses emerge from patient, methodical execution rather than visionary leaps.

2026-03-17.teaser: From Wall Street's surprising bet on coliving to the hidden architecture of enterprise software, this week's digest cuts through the noise to reveal where real money and power are moving. We explore why Goldman Sachs just made a statement acquisition, how AI might finally liberate us from legacy software hell, and the privacy battles brewing in your pocket. Plus, discover the NotebookLM features that could transform how you work with information. These aren't just tech stories—they're signals of fundamental shifts in how we live, work, and build.

included.title: Why the World Still Runs on SAP
included.summary: This a16z analysis cuts to the heart of enterprise software's biggest paradox: why Fortune 500 companies remain shackled to systems they openly despise. SAP, ServiceNow, and Salesforce dominate not through superior user experience—quite the opposite—but because they've become the digital DNA of modern business operations. The piece reveals the staggering costs of escape: SAP migrations can consume $700 million, three years, and armies of consultants, often resulting in systems that barely function beyond generating static reports. The insight here isn't just about legacy software's stickiness, but about AI's potential to fundamentally reshape this dynamic. Rather than wholesale replacement, the authors argue for a more nuanced future where AI becomes the intelligent interface layer, making these systems programmable and accessible while preserving the critical business logic embedded within them. This represents a massive market opportunity—not in building new systems of record, but in creating the control plane that makes existing ones actually usable. The winners will be platforms that first reduce migration risk and timeline, then expand into daily operations as trusted automation layers.

included.title: Goldman Sachs Just Bought a Coliving Company
included.summary: Goldman Sachs' acquisition of Urban Campus marks a watershed moment for the coliving industry, signaling its evolution from experimental housing model to institutional asset class. This isn't venture capital or private equity dabbling—it's one of the world's most sophisticated financial institutions making a permanent capital allocation to coliving operations. The timing is particularly striking, occurring as The Collective, once Europe's coliving darling, collapsed after failing to find a buyer, highlighting the sector's brutal consolidation phase. Meanwhile, Barcelona's coliving surge—a 900% increase in five years—has triggered mass protests and regulatory backlash, illustrating the tension between housing innovation and affordability concerns. The Goldman move validates what industry insiders have long argued: coliving's economics work at scale when properly executed. Urban Campus brings real assets, proven operations, and a track record across European markets—exactly the kind of mature platform that justifies institutional investment. For operators, this acquisition represents both validation and a new competitive reality where institutional capital will increasingly dominate. The message is clear: coliving has crossed the threshold from alternative experiment to mainstream real estate strategy, with all the opportunities and challenges that institutional backing brings.

included.title: Do banking apps really need all these permissions?
included.summary: Zerodha's founder Nithin Kamath delivers a pointed critique of banking app privacy practices, highlighting a fundamental contradiction in financial technology security. While most banking apps demand extensive device permissions—access to SMS, contacts, phone functions—in the name of security, Kamath argues this violates the Principle of Least Privilege, a cornerstone of cybersecurity best practices. His company's approach offers a compelling counter-narrative: Zerodha's Kite app requests zero permissions on mobile devices, relying instead on SEBI's mandatory two-factor authentication framework to balance security with privacy. This isn't just a technical debate—it's a philosophical one about trust, user agency, and the true nature of digital security. Kamath's position challenges the industry's permission-heavy approach, suggesting that robust security can coexist with minimal data access. The broader implications extend beyond banking to any app that claims security justifies invasive permissions. His 'golden rule' philosophy—don't do unto others what you don't want done unto you—offers a refreshing alternative to the surveillance capitalism model that dominates fintech. For millions of users who've grown accustomed to surrendering digital privacy for financial services, Zerodha's approach demonstrates that this trade-off isn't inevitable.

included.title: 3 Hidden NotebookLM Features Most People Don't Use
included.summary: This deep dive into NotebookLM's ecosystem reveals how Google's research tool transforms when connected to its broader AI infrastructure. While most users treat NotebookLM as a standalone research assistant, the piece explores three powerful integrations that unlock entirely new capabilities: Gemini Canvas for visual collaboration, Gems for persistent AI personalities, and Antigravity for automated research workflows. The author's previous work connecting NotebookLM to Claude via MCP focused on external integrations, but this exploration maps the internal Google ecosystem connections that many users overlook. These aren't just feature additions—they represent a fundamental shift in how AI tools can work together within a unified platform. Gemini Canvas turns research into visual, collaborative workspaces. Gems create specialized AI assistants that maintain context and personality across sessions. Antigravity automates the research pipeline itself, creating systems that continuously gather and process information. The implications extend beyond productivity hacks to suggest a future where AI tools form interconnected workflows rather than isolated applications. For power users, these connections transform NotebookLM from a research tool into a comprehensive knowledge management and creation platform, demonstrating how platform integration can multiply individual tool capabilities exponentially.
